A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DG-Mesh and contain complete main texts and supplementary material. Although v1 is image-only, its rendered text, equations, tables and figures are readable and support comparison with v3.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic reconstruction and rendering benchmarks, Laplacian and anchoring ablations, and real-scene reconstructions, including supplementary visual results.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, real-scene evaluations, efficiency measurements, controlled ablations and failure cases.

M1.justification: The architecture, reconstruction pipeline and main objectives remain the same. However, rewritten Algorithm 1 replaces explicit nearest-face matching with radius-based grouping and changes canonical-space updates, while the surrounding prose retains nearest-face anchoring. The PDFs do not resolve whether these differences represent intended procedural changes or inconsistent pseudocode.

E1.justification: v3 adds DyCheck smartphone videos, self-captured iPhone scenes and NeuralActor multiview human sequences. These substantially broaden real-world and capture-condition coverage. D-NeRF, the six-scene DG-Mesh dataset, Nerfies and Unbiased4D were already evaluated in v1; sphere-to-torus deformation is also retained coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds four evaluated Gaussian comparators: 4D-GS, Deformable-GS, 4DGS and SC-GS, while retaining the original four baselines. v3 also adds an Unbiased4D method comparison and a canonical-mesh deformation control. These substantially expand the comparison methods beyond v1's predominantly radiance-field baselines.

E3.justification: New protocols include 20,000-iteration mesh-loss fine-tuning of baselines, appearance comparisons using fixed DG-Mesh geometry, an anchoring-frequency sweep and mesh-query FPS evaluation. Appendix B changes the stated mesh-extraction onset from v1's supplementary 8,000 iterations to 5,000, matching the existing main-text setting without establishing reruns. Table 4 drops SSIM and LPIPS reporting.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained Laplacian and anchoring ablations, Appendices C–F test canonical-mesh deformation under topology change, baseline mesh fine-tuning, appearance modules on shared geometry and anchoring frequency. Appendix H and Figure 12 add explicit failure cases involving extreme motion or imperfect segmentation.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, standard deviations, confidence intervals or significance tests. The added experiments continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises DG-Mesh results across all six scenes and adds Gaussian-rendering PSNR and new baseline rows. For example, reported Bird mesh PSNR changes from 22.977 to 28.085, while Beagle changes from 34.518 to 33.572. Tables 5–8 and new galleries add results; Table 4 removes SSIM/LPIPS entries. Tables 2–3 remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The main Gaussian, deformation, Laplacian, anchoring and cycle-consistency equations retain their mathematical substance. Neither version presents theorems or proofs. The added topology and rendering discussions provide conceptual explanations rather than new formal results.

C1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction's novelty statement and conclusion broaden the framing from monocular videos to dynamic observations, accommodating multiview evaluation. The central contributions—temporally consistent meshes, Gaussian-Mesh Anchoring, topology flexibility and correspondence-enabled editing—remain intact.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations of surface versus volumetric appearance learning, rendering costs, anchoring-frequency tradeoffs and multiview benefits. DyCheck discussion explicitly qualifies applicability under extreme motion and imperfect segmentation. The original foreground-segmentation requirement and difficulties with major topology changes remain.

D1.justification: v3 adds a repository pointer and public code/data statement, real-video processing references, smartphone capture specifications and training-time estimates. Conversely, v1's Blender engine choices, 128 rendering samples, 800-by-800 sRGB specification and numerical anchoring search radius disappear. Network architecture and hardware were already documented. The conclusion retains the older future-release wording.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for SC-GS, 4DGS, Spacetime Gaussian Feature Splatting, DyCheck, NeuralActor and video segmentation, and removes the PyTorch citation. The two related-work themes and basic positioning relative to volumetric and template-based reconstruction remain largely unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much wording are retained, with localized clarifications of correspondence construction and training losses. v3 rewrites supplementary implementation and algorithm explanations, introduces an appendix contents list, reorganizes supplementary sections and moves the existing application discussion to Appendix N.

P2.justification: v3 adopts the ICLR layout, redraws the pipeline diagram, substantially revises comparison Figures 6–7, and adds real-scene, failure-case and ablation displays. Existing galleries are split and rearranged, and the application figure moves to the appendix. Tables gain comparator rows and new analyses; Table 4 loses metric columns. Figure 8 incorrectly captions the retained architecture diagram as reconstruction results.

improvement.justification: The expanded Gaussian comparisons and mesh-fine-tuning/shared-geometry controls substantially address v1's limited comparator coverage and uncertainty about geometry versus appearance advantages. Broader real-world and multiview evaluations, efficiency measurements and explicit failure cases strengthen assessment of applicability. These gains outweigh lost synthetic-generation details and remaining pseudocode/caption inconsistencies, although several new evaluations remain qualitative.
